look_here_first: Start with the leaves: most are conspicuously 3-lobed or deeply cut, with a long central lobe and smaller lateral lobes; then notice the coarse hispid/glandular plant and multiple terminal or axillary spikes.

project_inclusion.range_basis: 2026-10-14 corrected two-county status: Travis, Kerr inside 24-county zone; Williamson outside. Third accepted native county not yet established. Original evidence retained in range_audit.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: The project Hays native-source list does not include V. xutha, so Hays is not assumed from nearby Travis/Williamson occurrence.

range_audit.original_range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Verbena xutha and lists Texas within its native range. Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center has multiple Travis County Verbena xutha herbarium specimens. Williamson County — the UT Plant Resources Center field treatment documents Verbena xutha as part of the county flora. Kerr County — the Kerr WMA vascular flora documents Verbena xutha without an introduced marker.

best_field_traits: coarse perennial, one to several stems, commonly taller than V. canescens
stems and foliage hispid-hirsute with swollen/pustulate hair bases plus short glandular hairs
opposite leaves mostly 3-lobed or deeply cut, with the central lobe conspicuously dominant
leaf margins toothed and principal veins strongly raised below
flowers unevenly spaced along a ridged hairy rachis
morphology_keys.verbena_training: Separate these by leaf architecture + hair texture + spike/branching architecture before using flower color.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Verbena halei: Both can have divided leaves, but V. xutha is coarse and strongly hispid/glandular with a repeated 3-lobed leaf pattern; V. halei is more slender with highly variable lower pinnatifid leaves and very narrow upper leaves. Verbena canescens: V. canescens is short and uniformly gray-canescent with only short lobes; V. xutha is taller, greener/coarser, and strongly 3-lobed. Verbena brasiliensis: Brazilian vervain has simple narrow serrate leaves and an open many-branched panicle of short spikes rather than strongly lobed leaves.
